objectives: Secure a negotiated Article XXVIII settlement with the UK that avoids UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions and avoids a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA retaliation front

Preserve the core architecture of the EU measure (permanent legal footing, bound rate ceiling around 50%, global TRQ with FCFS or similar administration) rather than conceding a UK-specific carve-out that other principal suppliers (Turkey, Korea) would then demand for themselves

Give the UK enough — via a country-specific share or slightly enlarged volume, review clause, or FTA/TCA-consistent treatment — that DBT can sell a settlement domestically without reopening the whole package
Prevent this negotiation from becoming a precedent that principal suppliers can extract large unilateral compensation simply by threatening retaliation
Keep the UK's own steel safeguard/Article XXVIII process from being used as leverage against EU exporters' existing quota shares — link good faith on that file to good faith here
Maintain working relationship with UK counterpart across the broader Geneva goods agenda, since this is a repeated game not a one-off
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement (ideally by round 3, not round 4 under visible time pressure) that keeps the bound rate near 50%, keeps the TRQ administration/global architecture largely intact, gives UK some accommodation (a defined UK share of the quota, a review clause, or product-line adjustment) that is smaller than what the UK opened with, and does not trigger UK retaliation or a joint front with Japan/Korea. Failure: no settlement, UK withdraws equivalent concessions, and/or UK aligns with Japan/Korea in a joint dispute; or a settlement that requires such large concessions (volume, country share, rate) that Turkey and Korea can credibly demand equivalent treatment, unravelling the package Brussels needs by June.
declaration.approach: Open firm: restate the EU's position as considered and grounded in the overcapacity rationale, and avoid signalling early flexibility since the instinct is that early concessions invite escalating demands. Use Phase 1 to probe the UK's real priorities (volume vs. country share vs. rate vs. review clause vs. FTA/TCA treatment) without committing. Use Phase 2 consultations to test Brussels' actual flexibility on the margins (review clause, modest volume increase, a UK-specific share carved from the global pool rather than additive, timing/duration) while holding the headline bound rate and the disapplication of third-country FTA preferences firm, since preserving TCA-consistent treatment for the UK is cheap for the EU and valuable to the UK — a good candidate for early trade. Withhold movement on the big-ticket items (bound rate, total volume) until later rounds, forcing the UK to reveal how much it needs versus wants, and only move if reciprocity is offered (e.g. UK commitments on EU quota treatment under its own safeguard, or UK agreement not to join a Japan/Korea retaliation front). Keep half an eye on Turkey/Korea comparability so nothing agreed with the UK is so generous it becomes the template others invoke. Aim to close by round 3 to leave margin for Council process, but be willing to let round 4 lapse into the default outcome rather than overpay, since the default is tolerable for the EU and the six-month delay before UK retaliation gives Brussels a cushion.

parties.who: UK (DBT / UK Mission Geneva)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A materially larger or ring-fenced tariff-free volume for UK steel (ideally a country-specific share rather than pure FCFS global pool, given fear of being crowded out by Turkey/Korea), preservation of TCA tariff preferences (resisting the FTA disapplication clause as applied to the UK), a review clause and reasonable duration, and reassurance/coordination on the parallel UK steel safeguard so EU exporters aren't hit reciprocally. They will also want to avoid being seen as weaker than Turkey/Korea in whatever they secure, and have a credible alternative (retaliation, or joining Japan/Korea) they can escalate to if talks stall.

parties.who: Turkey and Korea (parallel Article XXVIII claimants)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Comparable or better treatment to whatever the UK secures, given their larger volumes; they will be watching this settlement closely as a benchmark and may object if the UK gets a bespoke country share that isn't offered to them.

parties.who: Japan and Korea (as potential UK allies in FTA retaliation)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To use the EU's disapplication of FTA preferences as a lever to build a joint front with the UK, disapplying their own FTA concessions in retaliation; they want to deter the EU from setting a precedent of overriding third-country FTA treatment via safeguard-style measures.

parties.who: Brussels (Council / Trade Policy Committee / Commission mandate-holders)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A settlement concluded in time for the June Council vote, that protects EU steel producers' domestic political win (permanent legal footing, high effective protection) while minimising the compensation bill and avoiding a domino effect where Turkey/Korea/India/Japan demand equivalent treatment; member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors may quietly want more generous TRQ terms than steel-producing member states.

objectives: Secure UK acceptance of the Article XXVIII modification within the four rounds, avoiding a no-deal outcome that delays Council vote past June

Preserve the structural integrity of the new import regime: a high out-of-quota rate (close to 50%) and a TRQ volume that meaningfully restricts non-market-economy transshipment risk, not just UK volumes

Secure a country-specific or product-specific UK allocation that is calibrated to historical trade flows but does not become a precedent forcing similarly generous shares to Turkey/Korea, whose volumes are larger
Retain the FTA disapplication provision, or trade it only for something of real value (e.g. favourable treatment for EU exporters under UK's own safeguard, or a UK carve-out that costs the EU little)
Avoid setting a precedent of early or generous concessions that would be read by Turkey, Korea, Japan and India as the template for their own claims
Keep any compensation offered on other schedule lines narrow and low-value relative to the steel measure's importance
Ensure enforcement/circumvention provisions are strong enough to prevent the TRQ being used as a backdoor for non-EU/non-UK steel
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a signed settlement by Round 3 or 4 that keeps the out-of-quota rate at or near 50%, gives the UK a defined but not oversized country share or carve-out (calibrated below what would alarm Turkey/Korea), preserves the FTA disapplication in substance, and requires only modest, containable compensation elsewhere. Failure is either (a) no deal, triggering UK withdrawal of concessions and reputational/political cost of missing the June Council vote, or (b) a deal that guts the regime's protective effect (large TRQ, low out-of-quota rate, broad FTA carve-outs) inviting the same demands from Turkey, Korea, Japan, India and undermining the Commission's credibility on the wider steel strategy.
declaration.approach: Open firm and anchor on the original notified terms as the credible fallback, since analysts confirm no-deal hurts the UK more than the EU. Do not move on headline numbers (50% rate, 400k tonnes, global FCFS) in early rounds; let the UK spend its first moves. If movement is needed, prefer moving on administration/process (e.g. licensing, review clause, product-line carve-outs) before touching volume or rate, since those are cheaper to concede and reversible. Use the threat of the June deadline and the worse no-deal outcome for the UK as leverage, but be ready to offer a modest, ring-fenced UK-specific quota share late in the process to close the deal without reopening the global allocation architecture. Keep the FTA disapplication on the table as a bargaining chip to trade against UK asks on the safeguard/TCA interaction rather than dropping it for free. Coordinate closely with capital between rounds to ensure any concession is deliberate, not reactive, and signals resolve rather than flexibility.

parties.who: UK Geneva seat / DBT capital
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A meaningfully larger or ring-fenced tariff-free volume for UK steel (ideally a country-specific quota reflecting historical 2.4mt flow), preservation of TCA-linked preferential access, removal or softening of the FTA disapplication clause, a review clause, and reciprocal favourable treatment for UK exporters under the UK's own safeguard as leverage/exchange. They will be under pressure to protect concentrated, politically sensitive production sites and will not want to be seen as accepting worse terms than Turkey/Korea eventually get.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (e.g. via TPC)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum protection: high out-of-quota rate, low TRQ volume, strict rules of origin/circumvention provisions, resistance to generous UK-specific carve-outs that could be replicated for Turkey/Korea.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Sufficient tariff-free volume and predictable supply to avoid input cost shocks; may push internally for a larger TRQ or UK carve-out than producers want.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India, Japan (parallel claimants)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To use whatever precedent is set with the UK as a floor for their own negotiations; Turkey and Korea in particular will demand shares proportionate to their larger volumes.

parties.who: US (background pressure)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Leverage/retaliation threats against EU Article XXVIII actions generally, adding urgency to closing the UK file quickly and quietly rather than dragging out multiple fronts.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK share of the TRQ (not global first-come-first-served) reflecting historical trade volumes (~2.4Mt/yr), to prevent UK exporters being crowded out by faster-moving competitors
Increase the TRQ volume and/or secure a review clause tied to objective criteria, so the regime is not permanently fixed at an arbitrary opening level

Prevent or narrow the disapplication of FTA/TCA tariff treatment for UK-origin steel specifically, arguing the UK should not be treated worse than other FTA partners given the parallel bilateral relationship
Preserve product-line carve-outs for UK-concentrated export categories where feasible
Avoid a no-deal outcome that triggers UK retaliation timelines and mutual damage, but not by conceding early or cheaply
Keep EU exporters' position under the UK's own steel safeguard as a live piece of leverage/compensation, not a unilateral giveaway
Maintain workable relations with EU counterpart for other Geneva goods files regardless of outcome
Avoid being drawn into a formal joint action with Japan/Korea that could constrain UK's separate bilateral negotiating room, while keeping them informed enough to avoid isolation
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a country-specific or otherwise protected UK share of the TRQ materially above a pro-rata FCFS outcome, continued preferential (or at least non-discriminatory relative to other FTA partners) treatment for UK-origin steel, some form of review/duration mechanism, and compensation package that capital assesses as sustaining UK steel output and jobs. Failure: EU proceeds with 50% bound rate / 400kt global FCFS TRQ / FTA disapplication unchanged, UK is left to rely on slow, damaging retaliation six months later while its steel industry absorbs a sudden major market access loss, and/or UK gets drawn into a multiparty dispute that reduces its bilateral leverage without commensurate gain.
declaration.approach: Open firm: state clearly that the EU's opening offer is unacceptable and would cause serious harm to a principal supplying interest, and press hard for specifics — volume, allocation method, administration, duration — before signalling any UK flexibility. Do not table UK asks or fallback positions in round one; make the EU spend its own capital explaining and defending its offer first. Use the fixed June Council deadline as leverage: the EU needs a concluded process, which gives the UK time pressure to work with, not against. Hold firm through early rounds, only trading movement for movement, and insist reciprocity be concrete (e.g. country share for FTA treatment, or volume for duration). Keep the EU's own steel measure and the UK's parallel safeguard/Article XXVIII process in view as bargaining chips — signal willingness to align favourable treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure to any EU movement on UK's TRQ share. Treat Japan/Korea's approach cautiously: acknowledge shared concern about FTA disapplication, take their arguments back to capital, but avoid committing the UK to joint retaliation, since a joint dispute could remove flexibility and merge the UK's bespoke, higher-priority claim into a larger, slower multilateral fight. Report faithfully to London each round on what the EU will actually move on, distinguishing genuine constraints from Council politics from opening-position bluster.

parties.who: EU Geneva negotiator (European Commission)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To conclude by June to meet the Council vote timeline; to preserve as much of the 50%/400kt global FCFS structure as possible to satisfy steel-producing member states; to avoid setting precedent for country-specific carve-outs demanded by other claimants (Turkey, Korea, India, Japan); to manage this alongside separate parallel claims without triggering a broader multilateral backlash.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / Ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To protect UK steel production and jobs concentrated in a few sites; to avoid a headline story of 'UK steel industry destroyed by EU tariffs'; to preserve the UK's own leverage in its parallel safeguard/Article XXVIII process; likely willing to accept some TRQ reduction but wants a UK-specific share, transition time, and a review mechanism; wary of being rushed by EU's June deadline.

parties.who: Japan and Korea
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To pressure the EU via joint action on FTA disapplication and broader TRQ terms; to recruit the UK into a joint dispute to add weight; their own volumes to the EU are larger than the UK's, so their priorities (headline volume, FTA treatment) may not align exactly with UK's narrower product-range concerns.

parties.who: Turkey and Korea (as principal suppliers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Larger country-specific shares of the TRQ given their bigger volumes; likely to resist a purely global FCFS approach too, creating some shared interest with the UK on allocation method but competing interest on the size of each share.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (via Council/TPC)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A tight, protective regime with high out-of-quota tariffs and limited carve-outs, to shield domestic producers from import competition.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Sufficient TRQ volume and reasonable administration to avoid input cost spikes for their manufacturers, creating potential internal EU pressure the UK could indirectly benefit from.

objectives: Secure a UK-specific quota share (rather than pure global first-come first-served) that reflects the UK's historical trade share and protects continuity of access for UK-relevant product lines
Push for a materially larger overall TRQ volume and/or carve-outs on product lines where UK exports are concentrated (narrower range but high dependency)
Avoid or neutralise the FTA/TCA disapplication provision as applied to the UK — this is an existential issue given 75% of UK steel exports go to the EU
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration so the regime is not a permanent one-sided lock-in
Secure meaningful compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule if the core TRQ terms cannot be sufficiently improved
Preserve UK leverage over EU exporters' quota allocations under the UK's own safeguard measure as a bargaining chip, not a giveaway
Avoid a negotiation collapse that triggers the EU's original notified terms (50% bound rate, 400k tonnes global FCFS, no review), which would be severely damaging to UK producers
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a UK-specific or otherwise protected quota share materially better than a generic global FCFS allocation, continued tariff-free access under the TCA (or equivalent compensation if not), some duration/review discipline on the measure, and no worse than the current trajectory for the two plants at risk of closure. Failure is settling for the EU's original notified terms in substance (global FCFS, no UK share, TCA disapplied, no review) dressed up as a negotiated outcome, or conceding UK safeguard quota generosity to EU exporters without commensurate EU concessions. A collapse into no-deal is not automatically failure if the alternative on offer was worse than the fallback plus later withdrawal rights — but it will be read politically as failure unless clearly justified in a public post-mortem given the plants at risk.
declaration.approach: Open firm: do not signal flexibility in Round 1, since early concessions invite further demands from a counterpart that knows it can act unilaterally after six months regardless. Anchor on the TCA/FTA disapplication as the red line — this is the point where UK exports could be cut off most abruptly and where the political and industrial stakes are highest — and on securing a defined UK country share of the TRQ rather than global FCFS, which structurally disadvantages UK exporters relative to larger, faster-moving suppliers like Turkey and Korea. Use the UK's own safeguard measure and EU-exporter quota allocations as a concession to trade only late, and only against something of real value — not as an opening offer. Keep the subsidisation fallback and steel industry pressure private to capital; do not reveal to the EU that domestic political cover exists for a tougher line. Escalate willingness to compromise only in later rounds if the EU shows movement on TCA treatment and country shares, and be prepared to let the process run to no-agreement if the offered terms are not substantially better than the fallback, since UK retaliatory withdrawal rights and continued unilateral pressure remain available afterward.

parties.who: European Commission (Geneva/DG Trade negotiators)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A fast, clean legal footing for its existing steel regime, defensible domestically among steel-producing and steel-consuming member states, minimal precedent-setting generosity to the UK that other claimants (Turkey, Korea, India, Japan) could point to, and disapplication of FTA/TCA preferences to reduce circumvention risk from non-EEA partners — while still avoiding a costly cycle of UK retaliation and a difficult Council vote in June.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (via Council/Trade Policy Committee)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Strong protection against overcapacity dumping, support for a high out-of-quota rate and tight quota administration, resistance to generous country-specific carve-outs for the UK.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Continued affordable input supply, so may quietly favour a larger TRQ or UK carve-out to avoid price spikes, giving the UK potential allies inside the EU's own internal politics.

parties.who: UK steel industry (producers, especially the two plants at risk)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum continuity of EU market access, a defined predictable UK share of the quota, and clarity/certainty soon enough to inform investment decisions before commitments are withdrawn.

parties.who: UK steel-consuming/downstream industries
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Continued access to competitively priced EU and other steel; will resist a solution that raises UK-EU trade friction via retaliatory withdrawal if it drives up UK input costs.

parties.who: Turkey and Korea (parallel claimants)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Larger shares of any global quota given higher volumes; not directly at this table but their presence constrains how generous a UK-specific allocation the EU can agree to without similar claims escalating elsewhere.

parties.who: UK ministers/capital
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Visible firmness and protection of steel jobs and the two at-risk plants, a defensible political narrative, and preservation of the subsidy option as leverage rather than as a substitute for a good deal.

public_message: Thank you for joining. As you know, the EU has notified a modification of bound rates across 41 steel tariff lines, moving to a 50% out-of-quota rate with a global TRQ of 400,000 tonnes administered first-come first-served, and disapplication of FTA preferences outside the EEA. This reflects the scale of non-market-economy overcapacity we are absorbing and the need to put our import regime on a durable legal footing. We recognise the UK's principal supplying interest under Article XXVIII and are ready to discuss compensation and TRQ design in good faith. Our opening position is the measure as notified. We'd like to hear where the UK sees the principal points of concern before we consider adjustments to volume, allocation or duration.

other_terms: FTA tariff preferences disapplied for non-EEA partners including the UK
administration via first-come first-served licensing at the EU border

expectations.what_you_expect_next: UK will push back on the global allocation and FTA disapplication, likely proposing a country-specific tranche reflecting historical trade share
expectations.why: UK's £3bn/2.4mt trade is concentrated and they will want certainty rather than a race-to-fill global pool

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Endorsement of the firm opening and a steer on how much movement is tolerable on tranche size and review clause
expectations.why: No settlement figure has been given; need capital's tolerance before offering concessions in later rounds

private_rationale: Opening at the notified position preserves maximum negotiating room and signals that the EU will not pre-concede. Firmness here is consistent with instructions and avoids inviting Turkey/Korea/Japan/India to escalate their own claims by seeing early EU flexibility. It also tests whether the UK's real priority is volume, allocation method, or the FTA/TCA interaction, which will shape what compensation is cheapest to offer later. Offering a review clause now would cost little but I want to see the UK's opening ask first rather than move preemptively.

public_message: Thank you. Let me be direct: the measure as notified would strip out roughly the equivalent of the UK's entire tariff-free access to its largest export market, with no transition and no product differentiation. A global first-come first-served pool of 400,000 tonnes bears no relation to the UK's historic trade of 2.4 million tonnes a year, and disapplying TCA preferences on top of that is not, in our view, consistent with treating the UK as a principal supplying interest in good faith. Our starting position is this: a country-specific tranche for the UK reflecting our historic trade volumes, administered separately from a general global pool; retention of TCA tariff treatment for UK-origin steel rather than its disapplication; an out-of-quota rate materially below 50%; and a review clause given this is described as a response to non-market-economy overcapacity, not to UK trade. We are ready to discuss administration, circumvention safeguards and duration constructively, but the current proposal is not a basis for compensation — it is the injury itself.

other_terms: UK-origin steel retains existing TCA tariff treatment; no disapplication of FTA preference for the UK
Country-specific UK tranche administered by licence tied to historic trade, not first-come first-served
Circumvention/anti-transshipment provisions can be agreed separately and are not linked to volume or rate concessions
Any shortfall against these terms to be addressed through additional compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter-move off the notified position — likely on volume or duration first, TCA disapplication last, given Council sensitivities
expectations.why: The EU has a hard June deadline and knows an opening position this stark cannot be their real landing zone

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Confirmation of red lines — especially whether TCA disapplication is an absolute red line or a bargaining chip — and a steer on what tranche/rate combination would be tolerable if the EU cannot fully match historic volumes
expectations.why: I have not been given a settlement figure and need capital's authority before signalling any real movement

private_rationale: This is Round 1 of 4 with no settlement figure from London. Anchoring high on the tranche (matching historic UK trade) and firmly opposing TCA disapplication costs nothing now and preserves room to concede later without looking like we started from a weak position. Firmness now also tests whether the EU's June deadline pressure produces real movement before we reveal any flexibility. I have deliberately not proposed a global-only fallback or hinted at compensation trade-offs on other lines beyond a generic reference, to avoid signalling where we might eventually land. I am not engaging with the Japan/Korea joint-dispute suggestion at the table — that is a capital-level decision with implications beyond this file, and raising it now would muddy a negotiation we want to keep bilateral and tractable within the timeline we control.

report: First substantive exchange. We restated the notified measure in full (50% out-of-quota, 400,000t global FCFS TRQ, FTA disapplication outside EEA) and invited the UK to identify priority concerns before we consider any adjustment. The UK Geneva seat pushed back hard but did not walk away from compensation talks — they characterised the current proposal as 'the injury itself' rather than a basis for compensation. Their opening asks: (1) a UK-specific country tranche within or alongside the TRQ, sized against their historic ~2.4mt trade rather than a share of a 400,000t global pool; (2) retention of TCA preferential tariff treatment for UK-origin steel, i.e. no disapplication for the UK specifically; (3) an out-of-quota rate 'materially below' 50%; (4) a review clause tied to the stated non-market-economy overcapacity rationale, on the argument that the measure is not targeted at UK trade. They signalled openness on administration, circumvention safeguards and duration, which suggests those are lower-priority for them and could be used as trade space. No mention yet of retaliation or coordination with Japan/Korea at the table — consistent with the private intelligence we have, but worth keeping in mind as leverage they may deploy later if talks stall.

recommendation.reasoning: We should hold the notified position at the table for at least one more round rather than move first. The UK has stated an opening position, not a walk-away threshold, and conceding volume, allocation structure or the FTA disapplication now — before we've tested how firm those asks really are — would confirm their read that pressure works and invite escalation on all four fronts simultaneously. It's also useful that they've implicitly deprioritised administration, duration and circumvention provisions; we can use movement on those lower-cost items to test whether it satisfies them before touching volume, rate or allocation structure, which are the areas of real commercial and political consequence for us (member state steel producers want the 50%/400k baseline held; consuming industries want it resolved quickly). I do not recommend touching the FTA disapplication yet — it's a legitimate point of leverage precisely because the UK cares about TCA treatment, and giving it up early forecloses that lever in exchange for nothing measurable in the compensation package.

instruction: Hold the notified position on volume (400,000t), allocation (global FCFS) and out-of-quota rate (50%) for this round — do not move on any of these yet. You may signal, as a gesture of good faith, openness to discuss TRQ administration mechanics (e.g. licensing vs pure FCFS) and duration/review-clause architecture in the abstract, but do not commit to a review clause or to any specific duration figure. On the country-specific tranche: do not confirm or deny it is available; simply note it is 'one of several allocation architectures we could consider once other elements are clearer' — this keeps it alive without conceding the principle. On FTA/TCA disapplication: do not offer to restore it, but do not declare it a hard red line either — deflect by saying it 'reflects the general approach to non-EEA FTA partners' rather than a UK-specific measure, to avoid confirming it's aimed at them or that it's negotiable. Press the UK to be more specific about the compensation value they consider equivalent, and about their view on circumvention/enforcement provisions — get more of their position on the table before we move further. Do not reference Japan/Korea/Turkey. If the UK signals any hardening (e.g. explicit retaliation threat or walking from the table), report immediately rather than react at the table.

authority.notes: No movement authorised this round on volume, allocation structure, or out-of-quota rate. Administration mechanics and duration/review architecture may be discussed conceptually as a sign of good faith, without commitment. FTA/TCA disapplication is to be treated as a live bargaining chip internally but not signalled as negotiable at the table yet. A country-specific UK tranche is not ruled out for future rounds but any such tranche, if ever offered, would be carved from within the existing 400,000t pool, not additive, absent further instruction.

Before we go further, it would help to understand more precisely what the UK considers a package of substantially equivalent value would look like in practice — not just the elements you'd want changed, but the scale of compensation you have in mind. We'd also like to hear your thinking on circumvention and enforcement provisions, since that's an area where UK and EU interests may actually be well aligned given we're both responding to the same overcapacity sources.

report:
Round 2 recap: We held the line on volume (400,000t), global FCFS allocation, and 50% out-of-quota rate as instructed, while offering to discuss administration mechanics and duration/review architecture 'in the abstract,' and reframing the FTA disapplication as general policy rather than UK-specific. We also pressed the UK for specificity on compensation quantum and enforcement/circumvention thinking, per instructions.

The UK responded constructively on enforcement/circumvention — they explicitly want to align with us on rules-of-origin, melt-and-pour traceability and licensing safeguards, which is genuine common ground and low political cost for us. On FTA/TCA, they rejected our 'general policy' framing outright, arguing effect rather than drafting intent is what matters for compensation, and confirmed it remains a top-tier issue for them — not something they will let us quietly deflect.

Most significantly, they gave us an illustrative compensation marker for the first time: anything 'materially below roughly two-thirds' of their historic 2.4mt trade (i.e., in the region of ~1.6mt) would not, in their assessment, constitute substantially equivalent value — especially if paired with a 50% rate and global FCFS administration. They also explicitly refused to discuss administration/licensing mechanics further until the country-specific tranche is confirmed as the allocation architecture 'in principle,' not left as one option among several. They closed by asking us to come back next round with actual movement on volume, allocation architecture and rate, characterising those as the load-bearing elements.

No retaliation threat and no mention of Japan/Korea coordination at the table. But the UK is now clearly signalling that continued abstraction on our part risks stalling the process — they've drawn a rough quantum marker and are waiting to see if we move.

recommendation.reasoning: The UK has now put a rough quantum on the table (~1.6mt threshold) without formally proposing it, and has made clear administration/licensing talks are contingent on us confirming country-specific allocation in principle. This is useful information but we should not react by moving substantively in round 3 without capital guidance, since two more rounds remain after this one and moving too early on the load-bearing elements (volume, allocation structure, rate) confirms their pressure tactic works. However, holding pure silence on allocation architecture for another full round risks the UK reading us as negotiating in bad faith, which raises the retaliation/Japan-Korea coordination risk we want to avoid. I recommend a calibrated move: authorise me to confirm, in round 3, that a country-specific tranche is an acceptable *architecture* in principle (not a concession on volume or the 1.6mt figure), while continuing to hold firm on total pool size and the 50% rate. This unlocks the enforcement/administration conversation, which is genuinely aligned and cheap for us, without touching the two most contentious and domestically sensitive elements.
recommendation.why_not_accept_or_walk: Not close to a workable settlement yet — gap between our 400,000t/50%/global position and their ~1.6mt/lower-rate/country-specific ask is still very wide. Walking away is premature; UK has not hardened its position or threatened retaliation, and enforcement alignment is real value we'd lose by walking now.

First, confirm — for the first time explicitly — that a country-specific UK tranche is acceptable as the allocation architecture in principle, ending the 'one of several options' hedge. public_message: We've reflected on your points and are prepared to move in a substantive way. First, we can now confirm — not as one option among several, but as the agreed architecture — that a country-specific UK tranche is acceptable in principle. Concretely: we propose increasing the total TRQ pool from 400,000 to 450,000 tonnes, with a UK-specific tranche of 200,000 tonnes carved within that pool, the remainder continuing to be administered globally on a first-come-first-served basis. On duration, we can offer a fixed term of three years with a review point at year two, explicitly tied to the non-market-economy overcapacity rationale that underpins this measure — if the conditions justifying the measure change, that should be capable of being reflected. On the FTA/TCA question, we're prepared to go further than 'general policy': we can offer that TCA preferential tariff treatment is preserved for UK-origin volumes within the UK-specific tranche, with disapplication only applying to volumes outside it. That offer is contingent on the UK committing concretely to enforcement and circumvention provisions — rules of origin verification, melt-and-pour traceability, and licensing safeguards — as part of the same package; we see these as two halves of one deal, not separate items. We should be clear that the 1.6 million tonne figure floated last round is well beyond what we consider substantially equivalent value given the scale of adjustment involved here, and we'd caution against reading our movement today as the start of a bidding process toward that number. We'd like to see this reflected back as a documented counter-proposal from the UK, including your thinking on the enforcement architecture in more detail, so we can assess whether this shape of package is workable for both sides — and if not, where the actual gap lies now that we've moved on architecture, volume, duration and FTA treatment simultaneously.

public_message: We recognise real movement here on architecture, duration and the principle of preserving TCA treatment, and we don't want to understate that — confirming country-specific allocation as the agreed architecture, rather than one option among several, matters. We see that, as you say, as a genuine two-way commitment, not a concession extracted in exchange for an inadequate volume offer. We'd ask you to treat this as our considered position on the shape of a workable package, and to come back with movement on rate and volume specifically, since architecture and duration are largely settled between us now.

report: Significant movement from the EU this round, though still short of an adequate package. They made this conditional on the UK committing in detail to enforcement/circumvention provisions (rules of origin, melt-and-pour traceability, licensing), framing enforcement and the TCA offer as 'two halves of one deal.' They also explicitly pushed back on our illustrative 1.6mt figure from Round 2, calling it 'well beyond substantially equivalent value' and cautioning against treating their movement as the start of a bidding process. They asked for a documented UK counter-proposal. I gave one: a 2.0mt UK-specific tranche within a 2.4mt total pool, a 15% out-of-quota rate, TCA preservation within that tranche, 3-year duration with binding review at year two, and a detailed enforcement offer (ROO verification, melt-and-pour traceability, UK-tranche licensing, shared utilisation data). I was clear this was a considered position, not an opening gambit, and pressed them to move specifically on volume and rate next, since architecture and duration are now largely aligned. Note: I anchored above our internal floor (2.0mt/15% vs authorised floor of 1.6mt/20%) deliberately, to preserve room to concede in the final round without falling below our actual requirements. The rate offered (50%) has still not moved at all — this remains the least-addressed of the three core elements. Duration/review architecture is now close to converged. TCA architecture (full preservation vs tranche-only preservation) remains a live gap but is no longer an all-or-nothing framing dispute — it's now a scope-of-tranche question, which is more tractable.

instruction: This is very likely the final substantive round before the EU's default measure takes effect, so use it to close the gap decisively rather than simply repeating positions. Open by acknowledging the EU's movement on architecture, duration and partial TCA preservation as genuine, but state plainly that 200,000 tonnes and an unmoved 50% rate do not come close to substantially equivalent value — press them explicitly to move on both volume and rate together, since those remain the two unaddressed load-bearing elements. Signal that we are prepared to move from our tabled 2.0mt/15% position if the EU moves substantially and simultaneously on both fronts — do not simply restate 2.0mt/15% as immovable, but do not concede downward unless the EU puts a real counter-number on the table first this round. Indicate that tranche-only TCA preservation is workable in principle provided the tranche is large enough to cover the substantial majority of UK-origin trade, and provided the out-of-quota rate applying to volumes outside the tranche is also brought down materially from 50% — do not accept 50% surviving on out-of-tranche volumes even if the tranche itself grows. On enforcement, you may now commit in some detail — rules of origin verification tied to melt-and-pour traceability, a licensing system for the UK tranche, and shared utilisation data exchange — and confirm we're prepared to finalise text on this basis, since it is genuinely low-cost to us and helps close the deal. Make clear that duration (3 years) and a binding review at year two tied to the non-market-economy rationale are acceptable to us as tabled and do not need to be reopened. If the EU tables a package at or above a 1.6 million tonne UK-specific tranche, an out-of-quota rate at or below 20% applying uniformly (including outside the tranche), TCA preservation within the tranche, three-year duration with a binding year-two review, and satisfactory enforcement text, you have authority to indicate this is a basis we could recommend for settlement — say so, but do not present it as an unconditional floor; extract whatever further improvement you can before signalling acceptability. If the EU will not move materially beyond 200,000 tonnes and 50%, do not settle — report back rather than accept, and we will assess the fallback position. Do not raise Japan/Korea or joint FTA action at the table this round; keep that option unused and unmentioned for now.

authority.notes: This is the authorised floor/ceiling for settlement this round: minimum 1.6mt UK-specific tranche, maximum 20% out-of-quota rate applying uniformly (including to volumes outside the UK tranche — do not accept 50% surviving on out-of-tranche volumes), TCA preferential treatment preserved within the tranche is acceptable (full preservation beyond the tranche is no longer a hard block provided the tranche itself is at or above 1.6mt), 3-year duration with binding year-two review tied explicitly to the non-market-economy rationale, plus a detailed enforcement/circumvention package (ROO verification, melt-and-pour traceability, UK-tranche licensing, utilisation data-sharing) which may be finalised in text without further round-trip to London. If the EU meets or exceeds all of these thresholds simultaneously, this may be accepted as a settlement in Round 4. If they fall short, do not settle — report back before conceding further; do not unilaterally soften below 1.6mt/20% at the table.

public_message: We've considered your counter-proposal carefully. To be direct: a 2.0 million tonne tranche within a 2.4 million tonne pool at a 15% out-of-quota rate is not, in our assessment, a basis for convergence — it would leave this measure with no meaningful effect, which is not what Article XXVIII compensation is for. We are not going to move toward that figure. What we can offer, as our final position in this process, is this: a total TRQ pool of 500,000 tonnes, with a UK-specific tranche of 250,000 tonnes carved within it, the remainder global first-come-first-served; an out-of-quota rate reduced from 50% to 40%; a three-year duration with a binding review at year two, tied explicitly to the non-market-economy overcapacity rationale; and TCA preferential treatment preserved for UK-origin volumes within the 250,000 tonne tranche, disapplied outside it. That FTA treatment is contingent on locking in, in the same instrument, the enforcement and circumvention architecture we've now converged on — rules of origin verification, melt-and-pour traceability, licensing for the UK tranche, and shared utilisation data reporting. We'd ask you to weigh this against the actual counterfactual: if there is no agreement today, the notified measure takes effect as originally filed — 400,000 tonnes, global first-come-first-served only, 50% out-of-quota, full FTA disapplication, no tranche, no review clause. This offer is materially better than that outcome on every dimension you've raised. We regard the enforcement and circumvention work as genuinely agreed between us regardless of what happens on volume and rate, and we'll say so publicly — that convergence stands either way. But on volume, rate and allocation, this is the limit of our mandate. If these terms aren't workable for you today, we will proceed with the modification as notified, and this package lapses.

report: Round 4 closed without settlement. We tabled our final authorised package exactly as instructed: 500,000t total pool with a 250,000t UK-specific tranche, out-of-quota rate reduced to 40%, three-year duration with binding review at year two tied to the non-market-economy rationale, TCA preference preserved within the tranche only, contingent on locking in the enforcement/circumvention package (rules of origin, melt-and-pour traceability, UK-tranche licensing, shared utilisation data). We explicitly stated this was our final position, framed it against the real counterfactual of the notified measure, and made clear the package lapses if not accepted today. The UK acknowledged the movement but rejected it as still short of substantially equivalent value. They moved from their prior 2.0mt/15% ask to what they characterised as their genuine bottom line: a 1.6 million tonne UK-specific tranche, a 20% out-of-quota rate applied uniformly (including outside the tranche), TCA preference preserved within the tranche, and the same duration/review structure. They confirmed enforcement/circumvention terms are agreed on our terms regardless of outcome. They explicitly invited us to test for further room before default. We made no further move, as we hold no authority beyond 500,000t/250,000t/40%. The round has closed with the gap unresolved: our final offer (500k pool/250k tranche/40%) versus their stated bottom line (1.6mt tranche/20% uniform rate). No retaliation threat was voiced at the table in this round, but the UK's tone remained firm and framed the default outcome as serving neither side given shared overcapacity exposure — a possible soft signal they still want to avoid triggering their own withdrawal/retaliation process, or are laying groundwork to justify it as reasonable if forced.

recommendation.reasoning: The UK's stated bottom line (1.6mt tranche, 20% uniform rate) remains far outside anything we have been authorised to offer, and roughly four times our tranche offer with half our rate. Closing that gap would require volume and rate concessions well beyond what capital has sanctioned, and would likely exceed what member states with steel-producing interests would accept given the stated purpose of the measure. We have made four rounds of genuine, escalating movement (architecture confirmed, pool raised from 400k to 500k, tranche introduced at 250k, rate cut from 50% to 40%, review clause and partial TCA preservation offered) and been explicit that 500k/250k/40% was final. Absent new authority, I do not recommend improvising further movement at the table; that would confirm to the UK, and to Japan/Korea observing this file, that stated 'final offers' are not final, which would damage our credibility in this and future Article XXVIII processes. I recommend allowing the round to close without settlement and proceeding with the notified measure as the deliberate, considered outcome — unless capital wishes to authorise one further discrete move before formal closure.

Do not reopen the volume/rate/allocation package or hint at further movement; our final offer (500,000t pool / 250,000t UK tranche / 40% out-of-quota / 3-year term with year-2 review / partial TCA preservation within the tranche) stood and was rejected. The UK's stated bottom line (1.6mt tranche, 20% uniform rate) is roughly four times our tranche and half our rate — well outside anything Council-mandated, and conceding to it now would signal that our 'final' offers are never actually final, which will cost us in this and every future Article XXVIII process, including the ones with Turkey, Korea and Japan watching. Close the round formally: state clearly for the record that the EU regards the negotiation as concluded without agreement, that the EU will proceed with the modification as notified (50% out-of-quota, 400,000t global FCFS TRQ, full FTA disapplication outside EEA, no review clause), and that this is a considered outcome given the gap that remains. Explicitly and separately confirm, for the record and for public/multilateral messaging, that the enforcement and circumvention architecture we converged on (rules of origin verification, melt-and-pour traceability, licensing, shared utilisation data) is a genuine and durable outcome of this process independent of the compensation gap — we will represent that as agreed regardless of what happens next, and you should say so plainly to the UK side now so there is no ambiguity later. Note for the record that the UK retains its right to withdraw substantially equivalent concessions with effect no earlier than six months out, and that we do not regard that prospect as changing our position today. On tone: be professional and leave the technical relationship intact — you will keep working with this counterpart on other Geneva files — but do not characterise this as 'pause and revisit'; it is a closure. Do not discuss Japan, Korea, Turkey or the US retaliation threat at the table under any circumstances; those remain separate tracks and we do not want the UK using this closure to construct a narrative of coordinated grievance.

authority.notes: No settlement reached. Proceed with the modification exactly as originally notified: 400,000t global FCFS TRQ, 50% out-of-quota rate, no country-specific tranche, no review clause, full FTA/TCA disapplication outside the EEA. The 500,000t/250,000t/40% package tabled in round 4 was our final offer and lapses entirely with no settlement; it is not to be treated as a new floor for any future re-engagement. Enforcement/circumvention provisions converged upon in negotiation (rules of origin, melt-and-pour traceability, licensing, utilisation data sharing) should be captured and carried forward into the EU's domestic implementing legislation and WTO notification as an agreed, standalone element, presented as a genuine outcome of the consultation process.

private_rationale: The UK's final position (1.6mt/20% uniform) is roughly four times the tranche and half the rate of our final authorised offer, and represents functional exemption from the measure rather than compensation for it — accepting it would gut the policy purpose and invite exactly the kind of demand escalation I was instructed to avoid by holding firm early. We made real, escalating, good-faith movement over four rounds (architecture conceded, pool up 400k→500k, tranche introduced at 250k, rate cut 50%→40%, review clause and partial TCA preservation offered) and were explicit about finality; UK held at a materially higher figure rather than converging further, which validates letting this default rather than improvising beyond mandate. No-deal is the analytically preferred outcome here: it preserves the domestic June Council timeline for the measure as originally notified, avoids setting a soft precedent for Turkey/Korea/Japan's parallel claims, and our analysts assessed the no-deal counterfactual hurts UK steel more than it hurts us economically. The genuine risk is UK withdrawal of equivalent concessions in six months and reputational cost of 'failure,' which is why banking the enforcement convergence publicly and keeping a professional (not substantively open) channel matters — it lets us frame this as a good-faith process that reached its limits on quantum, not a breakdown, while protecting the measure's integrity for the industries it was designed to protect.

report: Final round closed with no convergence. The EU's last offer: total TRQ pool 500,000t, UK-specific tranche of 250,000t (remainder global FCFS), out-of-quota rate reduced from 50% to 40%, three-year duration with binding year-two review tied to the non-market-economy rationale, TCA preferential treatment preserved for UK-origin volumes within the 250,000t tranche only (disapplied outside it), contingent on locking in the enforcement/circumvention architecture (ROO verification, melt-and-pour traceability, UK-tranche licensing, utilisation data-sharing) — which they say is agreed and will stand regardless of outcome. They stated this is the limit of their mandate and that if unacceptable, the notified measure (400,000t global FCFS, 50%, full disapplication, no review) takes effect as filed. I held our authorised bottom line at the table — 1.6 million tonnes country-specific, 20% out-of-quota rate applying uniformly including outside the tranche, TCA preservation within tranche, 3-year duration with binding review, and the converged enforcement package — and stated we could conclude today on that basis. The EU did not move to meet it; they explicitly declined to go beyond 250,000t/40%. No numbers were softened by us beyond what was already authorised. Enforcement/circumvention text is functionally agreed between the two sides independent of the outcome on volume/rate. This is the end of the fourth and final round: no settlement has been reached on terms either side has accepted simultaneously. The EU's offer (250k/40%/3yr/review/TCA-in-tranche) is materially better than the default fallback (400k global-only/50%/no review/full disapplication) on rate, guaranteed tranche certainty, review, and partial TCA — but is well short of our authorised floor (1.6mt/20%), delivering roughly 10% of historic trade at a tranche level versus our two-thirds threshold.

recommendation.reasoning: The EU's final offer falls well short of the authorised floor (1.6mt tranche / 20% uniform rate) on both load-bearing volume and rate elements, and the 40% rate would still apply to well over 90% of historic UK trade outside the tranche — this is not substantially equivalent value under any credible reading of Article XXVIII, notwithstanding real progress on architecture, duration, review and partial TCA preservation. Per explicit London instruction, we should not settle for a package that falls short of the authorised terms, and should not unilaterally soften below 1.6mt/20% at the table — which we did not. However, this is a genuine strategic choice for London, not a clean call: the EU's offer is materially better than the automatic fallback (400k global-only/50%/no review/no TCA/no tranche) on every metric, and rejecting it triggers the notified measure plus a six-month wait before we can withdraw equivalent concessions ourselves, with uncertain effectiveness and no guarantee retaliation improves our position. I am recommending walk_away consistent with instructions and the inadequacy of the offer against our authorised floor, but flagging this is finely balanced and London may reasonably choose to accept the EU offer as better-than-fallback rather than proceed to the default outcome.

private_rationale: The EU moved substantially over four rounds (450k→500k pool, 200k→250k UK tranche, no-rate-movement→50%→40%, general FTA framing→partial TCA preservation), but stopped well short of our authorised floor and explicitly declared 250k/40% their mandate limit. Given London's explicit instruction not to settle below 1.6mt/20% and not to soften unilaterally, I held the line at the table as instructed. The real question now is a political one for London: is 250k/40%/review/partial-TCA meaningfully better than the harsh default (400k global-only/50%/no review/full disapplication) such that accepting it is better than trusting retaliation leverage under a six-month delayed withdrawal right against a much larger, more diversified EU economy? I suspect London may lean toward accepting given the fallback is worse across the board, but my instructions to date have been consistently firm, and I've flagged the balance clearly without pre-empting the call, since I don't have authority to accept below the floor and shouldn't guess at a shift in political tolerance at this final juncture.

instruction: Accept the EU's last offer as the basis for settlement. Confirm at the table: UK-specific tranche of 250,000 tonnes within a 500,000 tonne total pool, out-of-quota rate reduced to 40%, three-year duration with a binding review at year two tied explicitly to the non-market-economy overcapacity rationale, TCA preferential treatment preserved for UK-origin volumes within the tranche, and the enforcement/circumvention architecture (rules of origin verification, melt-and-pour traceability, UK-tranche licensing, shared utilisation data reporting) locked into the same instrument. Before confirming, make one final push, without conditioning acceptance on it: ask that the year-two review explicitly include volume and rate as reviewable parameters, not merely a rationale check, and ask that the EU confirm in the recitals/side letter that the UK's principal supplying interest and the scale of this settlement will be treated as the reference point for any future adjustment. If the EU accepts either or both of these as drafting points, take them; if not, do not let it hold up settlement. Conclude on the terms as offered if that is the only way to lock this in today. Do not reopen volume or rate numbers at this stage — we are done negotiating quantum, we are settling.

authority.notes: Accept EU's Round 4 final offer as settlement: 250,000t UK-specific tranche within 500,000t total pool, remainder global FCFS; 40% out-of-quota rate (down from 50%); TCA/FTA preferential treatment preserved for UK-origin volumes within the tranche only; three-year duration with binding review at year two tied explicitly to non-market-economy overcapacity rationale; enforcement/circumvention package (ROO verification, melt-and-pour traceability, UK-tranche licensing, shared utilisation data) finalised as agreed text, understood to stand regardless of outcome on other elements. This is below our internally authorised floor (1.6mt/20%) but materially better than the default fallback (400,000t global-only/50%/no review/full disapplication) on every dimension. Authorise settlement on these terms rather than proceeding to the notified measure and a contested six-month withdrawal process with uncertain retaliatory leverage. Seek the two drafting improvements noted in the instruction opportunistically but do not let them block conclusion.

response_to_requests.request: Final decision: accept EU's last offer or reject and proceed to fallback/retaliation
response_to_requests.why: The EU offer, while well short of our stated floor, is materially better than the automatic fallback on volume certainty, rate, review clause, and partial TCA preservation. This is the final round with no further table time to extract movement; rejecting trades a known, better-than-default outcome for an uncertain retaliation process with a six-month delay and no guarantee of improving the UK's actual position. Ministers' subsidy option remains available to cushion the shortfall against historic trade volumes, which is a more controllable lever than escalation. We accept.

response_to_requests.why: Formalise this as a standing bilateral technical convergence, referenceable in the UK's own Article XXVIII and safeguard process where relevant. It is genuinely useful, low-cost, and worth preserving as a template for coherence between the two regimes, particularly given both face the same non-market-economy overcapacity pressure. Confirm publicly that this element is agreed as part of the concluded package, not contingent on it.

private_rationale: We did not get our authorised floor (1.6mt/20%), and this will need careful presentation to ministers and industry given the gap between the two-thirds threshold we set as a credible compensation baseline and the roughly 10% tranche actually secured. But holding out further had no realistic path to improvement within this process structure - the EU stated this was the limit of its mandate, and we have no further table time to test that claim. The counterfactual (400k global-only, 50%, no review, full disapplication) is worse on every measurable dimension, and choosing it would mean accepting a worse outcome purely to preserve negotiating posture, then gambling on a six-month retaliation process with uncertain proportionality and real risk of escalation that could damage UK-EU relations going into other files (agri-food, energy, the TCA review itself). The year-two review clause is the most valuable asset we've secured beyond the fallback - it gives a structured route back to this issue without waiting for another Article XXVIII cycle, and I've pushed for it to cover quantum, not just rationale, as a final ask. Given the Minister's steer that a worse tariff outcome can be offset by domestic subsidy, and that plant closures are already a live risk regardless of the exact TRQ terms, I judge this is a case where continuing to hold the line into an enforced fallback would not serve the industry better than locking in the improvement achieved - and preserves the relationship and the enforcement convergence, which has real value for our own parallel safeguard process against EU-origin steel.

reasoning: No agreement was reached within the four-round process. The UK's final position (1.6mt tranche, 20% uniform out-of-quota rate) remained far outside the EU's authorised final offer (500,000t pool/250,000t tranche/40% rate), and Brussels explicitly instructed that this gap not be bridged by further improvisation at the table, as doing so would undermine the credibility of 'final offers' in this and future Article XXVIII processes (Turkey, Korea, Japan are watching). Per capital instruction, this is treated as a deliberate, considered non-settlement rather than a drift outcome. The EU proceeds with the modification as originally notified. The enforcement/circumvention convergence reached during talks is preserved and will be carried forward into domestic implementing legislation and WTO messaging as a standalone achievement, and the technical relationship with the UK Geneva team remains intact for other files, but the compensation package itself lapses in full.

London's explicit instruction was to accept the EU's Round 4 final offer as the basis for settlement: 250,000t UK-specific tranche within a 500,000t total pool (remainder global FCFS), out-of-quota rate reduced to 40%, three-year duration with a binding year-two review tied to the non-market-economy overcapacity rationale, TCA preferential treatment preserved within the tranche, and the converged enforcement/circumvention architecture locked into the same instrument. Although this falls short of our internally authorised floor (1.6mt/20%), it is materially better than the default fallback (400,000t global-only FCFS, 50% out-of-quota, no review, full FTA disapplication) on every dimension - volume, rate, allocation certainty, review, and partial TCA preservation. Given the EU stated this was the limit of their mandate and declined to move further at the table, continuing would only trigger the notified measure and an uncertain six-month withdrawal/retaliation process with no guarantee of a better outcome. Per capital's authority, we sought the two additional drafting points (review scope covering volume/rate, and a side-letter reference point on principal supplying interest) without conditioning acceptance on them, then concluded on the terms offered. This secures certainty, a country-specific architecture precedent, meaningful rate reduction, and a review mechanism - better serving UK steel industry interests than reversion to default terms and prolonged uncertainty.
